un fruscio vago e legger;: Bardolfo describes the soft whispers behind the screen, misinterpreting Fenton and Nannetta's tender reconciliation as Falstaff wooing Alice. Note the poetic apocope 'legger' for 'leggero'.
è la voce della donna: it is the voice of the woman
Bardolfo assumes the feminine whisper behind the screen belongs to Alice Ford, confirming to his conspirators that the rendezvous is underway.
Relative clause modifying 'donna'. Bardolfo uses the mock-heroic title 'cavalier' to refer to Falstaff, unaware of who is truly hiding behind the screen.
Odi come amor lo cuoce!: Pistola relishes Falstaff's supposed passion with the culinary metaphor 'amor lo cuoce' (love is cooking/burning him), highlighting the comic dramatic irony.
Pistola creates a high-flown mythological simile, comparing the fat knight pursuing Alice to the river god Alpheus relentlessly pursuing the nymph Arethusa.
Quella gonfia cornamusa: Pistola mocks Falstaff's corpulent physique by comparing him to an overinflated bagpipe ('gonfia cornamusa') wheezing out romantic sighs.
sends forth a tiny thread of voice.
The idiom 'un fil di voce' denotes an extremely faint or hushed whisper, comically contrasting with the enormous physical bulk of the 'cornamusa'.

Ma fra poco il lieto gioco.meaning: shortly / in a little while / soon

Ma fra poco il lieto gioco: Pistola relishes the impending catastrophe awaiting the lovers. 'Fra poco' acts as a temporal adverbial indicating swift retribution.
Inverted syntax: the subject 'dura lezion' (with apocope of 'lezione') follows the transitive future verb 'turberà', whose direct object was 'il lieto gioco'.
Egli canta, ma fra poco: Pistola scoffs at Falstaff's romantic song ('egli canta'), anticipating the rude shock when Ford corners him.
Idiomatic Italian 'mutare canzone' corresponds to English 'to change one's tune', foreshadowing Falstaff's screams when surprised.
QUICKLY E MEG: Libretto character heading marking the duet between Meg Page and Mrs. Quickly as they stand guard over the laundry basket.

Sta' zitta! Se ridi,.meaning: stay / be (2nd sing. imperative, apocope of stai)

Sta' zitta! Se ridi,: Meg urges Quickly to keep composure. 'Sta' zitta' pairs the truncated imperative of 'stare' with the feminine predicative adjective 'zitta'.
Meg warns that uncontrollable giggling will expose their elaborate prank ('burla') before Ford can be taught his lesson.
We must stay on the alert.

Dobbiam stare all'erta..meaning: we must (1st plural present, apocope of dobbiamo)

The modal verb 'dobbiam' (poetic apocope of 'dobbiamo') governs the idiomatic phrase 'stare all'erta' (to remain vigilant / keep guard).
Meg cautions Quickly that laughing out loud risks throwing their finely calibrated plot off course ('disguidi', from 'disguidare').
Geloso marito,: Meg summarizes the moral symmetry of their plot: punishing Ford, the pathologically suspicious 'geloso marito'.
compare sfacciato,: 'Compare sfacciato' refers to Falstaff, whose brazen audacity in attempting to seduce both married women has earned him this ordeal.
ciascuno è punito: Passive construction expressing poetic justice: both the jealous husband and the insolent rogue receive retribution.
Meg delivers the core ethical moral of the comedy: each character's punishment perfectly matches the nature of their fault (contrapasso).
Parliam sottovoce: Let us speak in a whisper

Parliam sottovoce.meaning: let us speak (1st plural hortatory subjunctive, apocope of parliamo)
in a whisper / in an undertone

Parliam sottovoce: Hortatory subjunctive 'parliam' urging Meg and Quickly to converse only in a hushed whisper as they watch over the basket.

guardando il messer.meaning: gentleman / sir (archaic title, apocope of messere)

guardando il messer: The gerund 'guardando' expresses simultaneous action. 'Messer' is used with biting irony for the suffocating knight.
che brontola e cuoce: Meg describes Falstaff's physical and verbal agitation inside the laundry hamper, resuming the recurring culinary motif ('cuoce').
Apocope of 'paniere' to 'panier' to preserve meter and rhyme with 'messer'. The women claim proud ownership of the entrapment device.
Stiam zitte! stiam zitte!: Let us be quiet! let us be quiet!

Stiam zitte! stiam zitte!.meaning: let us stay / be (1st plural hortatory subjunctive, apocope of stiamo)

Stiam zitte! stiam zitte!: Quickly repeats the injunction to stay quiet, agreeing with Meg in the feminine plural 'zitte'.

Trattieni le risa;.meaning: laughter (irregular feminine plural of il riso)

Trattieni le risa;: Imperative 'trattieni' governing the poetic feminine plural 'le risa' (bouts of laughter), urging Meg to suppress her giggles.

se l'altro s'avvisa.meaning: becomes aware / notices (3rd sing. present reflexive)

se l'altro s'avvisa: Literary reflexive 'avvisarsi' (to become aware / perceive). 'L'altro' refers to Ford, who is prowling nearby.
Quickly highlights the danger: discovery before their trick is sprung would spell total defeat for their plan.
Costui suda e soffia,: Quickly paints a vivid picture of Falstaff's physical misery under the mountain of dirty laundry with the alliterative 'suda e soffia'.

s'intrefola e tosse,.meaning: squeezes in / burrows in / wriggles (3rd sing. present reflexive)

s'intrefola e tosse,: The rare Tuscanism 'intrefolarsi' (to burrow or wriggle into narrow spaces) conveys Falstaff's desperate squirming; 'tosse' is an archaic present of 'tossire'.
per gran battisoffia: 'Battisoffia' is a colorful, dialectal Tuscan term for a sudden fluttering of the heart or panic, compound of 'battere' and 'soffiare'.
Inverted word order: 'le viscere ha scosse' emphasizes the physical, gut-wrenching terror experienced by Falstaff.
Costui s'è infardato: Reflexive verb 'infardarsi' literally means to soil or plaster oneself with filth, here denoting both the filthy linen and moral degradation.
Complements 'infardato': Falstaff has disgraced himself through shameless cowardice and dishonorable conduct.
Che darlo al bucato: That giving him to the laundry

Che darlo al bucato.meaning: to give him (infinitive dare + direct object clitic lo)

Che darlo al bucato: Enclitic construction 'darlo' (dare + lo). Quickly makes a comic pun on 'bucato': giving him to the wash cleanses both his clothes and his morals.
is to have pity on him.

è averne pietà..meaning: to have ... of him (infinitive avere + clitic ne)

The clitic particle 'ne' represents 'di lui' ('averne pietà' = to take pity on him). Quickly facetiously frames dumping him in the river as an act of mercy.
Come in sua zolla: Opening simile of Nannetta's lyrical canzonetta behind the screen, contrasting delicate youthful romance with the farcical chaos outside.
si schiude un fior,: Reflexive verb 'schiudersi' paired with the apocopated subject 'fior', portraying the budding of love like a spring flower.
la sua corolla: Botanical noun 'corolla' continues the floral imagery, representing the blooming petals of the heart.
Lyrical verb 'svolvere' (to unfold/open up) paired with the poetic apocope 'cor' for 'cuore'.
Bocca mia dolce!: Fenton's passionate exclamation as he kisses Nannetta behind the screen, echoing the opening sonnet of the opera.

Pupilla d'or..meaning: of gold (preposition di + apocopated noun oro)

Poetic synecdoche: 'pupilla' for eye, adorned with the golden brilliance of youth and love.
Voce che molce: Archaic and highly poetic verb 'molcere' (to soothe, soften), derived from Latin mulcere, evoking classical Italian love lyric.

com'arpa il cor..meaning: like a harp (elided come + noun arpa)

Simile comparing the beloved's voice soothing the heart to the sweet strumming of a harp.
Gente del vicinato: Choral designation in the score indicating the group of neighbors and retainers joining Ford's armed search.
Piano, piano, a passo lento,: The stealthy advance of the men creeping toward the screen in hushed suspense, underscored by Verdi's ticking staccato rhythm.
mentr'ei sta senza sospetto: Contraction 'mentr'ei' (mentre + archaic pronoun ei). The men erroneously assume the quarry behind the screen is completely off-guard.
lo cogliamo a tradimento,: Idiomatic locution 'a tradimento' denotes catching someone by unawares ambush or surprise.

gli facciamo lo sgambetto..meaning: trip / tripping (fare lo sgambetto = to trip someone up)

Colloquial idiom 'fare lo sgambetto' (to trip someone up), expressing their eager intent to topple their rival.
S'egli cade più non scappa:: If he falls, he escapes no more:
Hypothetical clause 's'egli cade' leading to the triumphant conclusion that the trapped man will have no avenue of flight.
no one can save him anymore.

nessuno più lo può salvar..meaning: can / is able to (3rd sing. present)

Negative pronoun 'nessuno' with the modal 'può' governing the apocopated infinitive 'salvar'.

Nel tuo diavolo t'incappa;.meaning: run into / stumble into (2nd sing. imperative reflexive)

Nel tuo diavolo t'incappa;: A curse or imprecation: 'incapparsi nel diavolo' means to run headlong into destruction or one's own undoing.
che tu possa stramazzar!: may you crash to the ground!

che tu possa stramazzar!.meaning: to crash down / collapse heavily (apocope of stramazzare)

che tu possa stramazzar!: Optative subjunctive expressing a vindictive wish: 'stramazzare' vividly denotes crashing flat to the floor with a violent thud.
Hush! To us! This is the moment.
Ford hushes his companions and gives the battle cry 'A noi!' as they prepare to overthrow the screen.
Hush! Pay attention! Pay attention to me.

Zitto! Attenti! Attenti a me..meaning: attentive / watchful (plural adjective used as command)

Ford coordinates the attack with military seriousness, commanding everyone to watch his signal.

Da' il segnal..meaning: give (2nd sing. imperative, apocope of dai)

Dr. Caius urges Ford to give the signal. Note the truncated imperative 'Da'' and apocopated noun 'segnal'.
Ford counts down with breathless tension. On 'Tre', the men violently topple the screen.
Non è lui!: Dr. Caius cries out in shock upon discovering young Fenton instead of Falstaff behind the fallen screen.
Sbalordimento!: Exclamatory noun sung by all the men, capturing their utter paralysis of surprise at finding the wrong man.
QUICKLY, MEG, ALICE E FALSTAFF: Libretto character heading refocusing attention onto the laundry basket across the room.
Ouff!... Cesto molesto!: Falstaff pops his head up from the dirty linen, groaning in rhyming exasperation ('cesto molesto') as he suffocates.
Silenzio!: Alice frantically pushes Falstaff's head back under the linen, terrified that his groans will alert Ford.
Protesto!: Falstaff pops up again indignantly; the rapid rhyme 'molesto / protesto' accentuates the farcical jack-in-the-box staging.
Che bestia restia!: Meg and Quickly compare the struggling Falstaff to a balking, recalcitrant beast resisting confinement.

Portatemi via!.meaning: carry me / take me (imperative 2nd plural portare + enclitic mi)

Portatemi via!: Falstaff desperately pleads to be carried anywhere to escape suffocation, ironically setting up his plunge into the river.
È matto furibondo!: Meg humorously brands Falstaff's frantic thrashing as sheer madness ('matto furibondo').
Aiuto!: Falstaff's muffled cry for help as the women pile more dirty sheets over his face.
È il finimondo!: It is the end of the world!

È il finimondo!.meaning: end of the world / bedlam / utter chaos

È il finimondo!: The women exclaim at the total pandemonium ('finimondo') unfolding as the farcical cross-purposes collide.
Dolci richiami: Nannetta and Fenton continue their lyric love song, blissfully detached from the uproar around them.

d'amor..meaning: of love (preposition di + apocopated noun amore)

Continuation of 'Dolci richiami': love's sweet summonses. Apocope of 'amore' to 'amor'.

Te bramo!.meaning: I crave / yearn for (1st sing. present)

Te bramo!: Fenton places the object pronoun 'Te' first for romantic emphasis before the passionate verb 'bramo'.
Dimmi se m'ami!: Tell me if you love me!

Dimmi se m'ami!.meaning: you love me (clitic mi + 2nd sing. present ami)

Dimmi se m'ami!: Fenton demands reassurance with the imperative 'Dimmi', introducing the indirect question 'se m'ami'.

Sì, t'amo!.meaning: I love you (clitic ti + 1st sing. present amo)

Sì, t'amo!: Nannetta's tender declaration of love, answering Fenton's plea with unequivocal devotion.

T'amo!.meaning: I love you (clitic ti + 1st sing. present amo)

T'amo!: Fenton's passionate echo right as Ford turns around and catches them in the act.

Ancor nuove rivolte!.meaning: yet / still / once more (apocope of ancora)

Ancor nuove rivolte!: Ford explodes in fury at Nannetta, perceiving her clandestine romance with Fenton as insubordination against his paternal will.

Tu va' pe' fatti tuoi!.meaning: your own business / your own affairs

Tu va' pe' fatti tuoi!: Ford rudely chases Fenton away with the colloquial idiom 'andare pe' fatti propri' (mind your own business / be off).
L'ho detto mille volte: «Costei non fa p: I have said it a thousand times: "This girl is not for you".

L'ho detto mille volte: «Costei non fa p.meaning: is suited for / is right for

L'ho detto mille volte: «Costei non fa p: Ford reiterates his stubborn refusal to give Nannetta to Fenton ('non fa per voi'), using formal 'voi' to Fenton and disparaging 'costei' for his daughter.

È là! Ferma!.meaning: stop / halt (2nd sing. imperative or 3rd sing. present)

È là! Ferma!: Bardolfo creates a diversion by shouting that he spotted the fugitive heading towards the stairs.
FORD Dove?: Ford's manic attention immediately snaps back to his prime obsession: catching Falstaff.
Là!: Pistola backs up Bardolfo's feigned sighting, pointing urgently toward the back staircase.
Bardolfo directs the entire mob up the stairs, clearing the room for Alice to carry out her plan.

FORD Squartatelo!.meaning: quarter him / hack him to pieces (imperative squartate + clitic lo)

FORD Squartatelo!: Ford's bloodthirsty command ('squartate' + clitic 'lo') demonstrates the extreme pitch of his manic jealousy.
PISTOLA, BARDOLFO, DR. CAJUS, I COMPAGNI: PISTOL, BARDOLPH, DR. CAIUS, THE COMPANIONS
Libretto heading indicating the mob of men roaring 'A caccia!' as they charge upstairs.
Che caccia infernale!: Mrs. Quickly watches the chaotic scramble of men with amused irony, comparing it to an infernal hunt.
Ned! Will! Tom! Isaac! Su! presto! prest: Ned! Will! Tom! Isaac! Come! quick! quick!
Alice calls her servants by their English names (taken straight from Shakespeare), urging them to hurry while the men are upstairs.
Rovesciate quel cesto: Alice gives the decisive order to hoist and dump the laundry basket containing Falstaff.
from the window into the water of the ditch.
Alice designates the destination: the ditch outside the window leading into the River Thames.
Là! Presso alle giuncaie,: 'Giuncaie' refers to the reeds and rushes growing along the riverbank.
in front of the gathering of the washerwomen.
Alice deliberately aims for the gathering ('crocchio') of washerwomen to maximize Falstaff's public humiliation.
TUTTE: Choral heading for all four women (Alice, Meg, Quickly, Nannetta) singing in triumphant unison.
Sì, sì, sì, sì!: Rapid, joyful affirmation from the women cheering on the servants' heavy work.
There is a big shot inside.
Nannetta jokes with the straining servants; 'pezzo grosso' is a pun meaning both a physically huge item and a VIP/bigwig.
Alice sends the young page to fetch Ford so that he will witness the spectacle of Falstaff floundering in the water.
We shall tell him our mad story.

Gli narreremo il nostro caso pazzo..meaning: we shall recount / tell (1st plural future)

Alice plans to reveal the whole crazy plot ('caso pazzo') to Ford, clearing her name and exposing his foolish jealousy.
Solo al vedere il cavalier nel guazzo: Merely upon seeing the knight in the water

Solo al vedere il cavalier nel guazzo.meaning: to see / seeing (substantivized infinitive al vedere = upon seeing)

Solo al vedere il cavalier nel guazzo: 'Nel guazzo' (in the slosh/water). Alice knows the ridiculous sight of Falstaff soaking in the Thames will dissolve Ford's wrath.
of every jealous whim he will be cured.
'Ubbia' denotes an irrational prejudice or fixed paranoia. Ford's jealousy will be cured by comic humiliation.

Pesa!.meaning: it weighs / it is heavy (3rd sing. present)

Pesa!: Quickly exclaims at Falstaff's colossal weight as the four servants strain to lift the basket.
Coraggio!: Alice and Meg encourage the straining servants as they heave the basket toward the open window.
Il fondo ha fatto crac!: Nannetta notices the basket's wicker base groaning and cracking under Falstaff's tremendous bulk.
NANNETTA, MEG E QUICKLY: Score heading indicating Nannetta, Meg, and Quickly shouting together for the final heave.
Su!: The women shout the final coordinated heave to flip the basket over the window ledge.
Trionfo!: Alice's exultant cry as the basket teeters on the window frame ready to plunge.
Ah! Ah!: Explosion of communal laughter as Falstaff and the dirty laundry tumble into the air.
Che tonfo!: Alice describes the monumental splash and thud as Falstaff hits the water below.
E MEG Che tonfo!: Meg joins Nannetta echoing Alice's delight at the resounding splash; includes score speaker indication 'E MEG'.
Patatrac!: The famous comic onomatopoeic finale of Act 2, as the entire household dissolves into uncontrollable, roaring laughter.
